articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to nominate their favorite tree to become a City of Piedmont Heritage Tree. To nominate a tree or group of trees from Piedmont’s parks and public spaces, residents can complete an online nomination form by Friday, March 21. It’s easy to see a smudge on your neighbor’s face and be oblivious to the ugly sneer on your own. Do you have the nerve to say, “Let me wash your face for you,” when your own face is distorted by contempt? It’s this I-knowbetter-than-you mentality again, playing a holier-than-thou part instead of just living your own part. Wipe that ugly sneer off your own face and you might be fit to offer a washcloth to your neighbor. (Luke 6:41-42) This is important counsel. While we are to be discerning, we are not to be judgmental. We are to be as aware of the obstacles to our own perception as we are of the shortcomings of others. We are recognize that the advice we are so ready to give may not be as helpful in every situation as we think it is. I hear Jesus saying that it is a sin to be arrogant, to be unaware of our imperfection, to believe that we are fundamentally superior to the other human beings with whom we share this planet. That being noted, while it is a sin to be arrogant and unaware, it is also a sin be naïve, to think that we can only speak, act or lead when we have achieved perfection ourselves. In his book The Wounded Healer the great teacher Henri Nouwen puts it this way. “Nobody escapes being wounded. articles.text: Editor: I went to the City’s Objective Design Standards (ODS) Open House last week. It was billed as a presentation demonstrating how the ODS were being tailored just for Piedmont’s SB 9, ADU and other City projects, and were intended to provide “clear and consistent expectations of high-quality design for new projects in Piedmont”. But it came off to me as a sales pitch indicating that the City has embraced the State’s SB 9 regulations that will no doubt destroy the wonderful urban beauty and texture of Piedmont that has existed for over 100 years. In response to the State’s SB 9 heavy handedness, Piedmont has augmented and created its own Division 17.54 Urban Lot Split and Two-Unit Housing Development regulations to work in conjunction with the State’s SB 9. However, I believe there are things the City can do to mitigate some of the negative issues associated with SB9/Division 17.54. SB 9 and the City’s Division 17.54 are a developer’s delight. In tandem they will destroy the unique character of each and every single family home neighborhood in Piedmont. They take away hearings and reviews by the Planning Commission and the City Council. There is no public notice about an upcoming SB 9/ Division 17.54 project. I came away from last week’s meeting thinking that the effort was like putting lipstick on a pig. SB 9/ Division 17.54 have just a very minimum ministerial review by the Planning Director based on a few planning/zoning standards that in turn, result in a process that is unfair to Piedmont’s residents. Combined together, SB 9 and Division 17.54 are very deceptive regulations. Here’s an example of why SB 9 is a dangerous and unfair law. A Building Permit Review is the place where a project gets looked at for health and safety impacts. Under SB 9/Division 17.54, a project is reviewed for a Building Permit in the 2nd part of a project’s process. But to get to this 2nd part health and safety review, the project must first get approved for a Lot Split and a 2 Two Unit Development. It’s also important to understand that once a project gets this 1st part approval, it’s all downhill for a neighborhood because the developer can go to the County and file for a tentative parcel map. So, where there was once only one parcel, there are now two and a Building Permit is just around the corner. SB 9/ Division 17.54 would like people to think a project can be denied for health and safety impacts, but it requires this very review for health and safety to occur after the project gets approved for a lot split and along with the right to build up to 4 residential units. This is a little bit outrageous. Again, SB 9 and Division 17.54 do not protect Piedmont’s resiproject clearly doesn’t meet current Piedmont and California Building and Fire code safety and health standards. I say this as a retired architect who is familiar with these regulations. I’ve lived on Nace Avenue for 35 years and I’ve seen 6 attempts by developers to put something on the 210 Howard Flag Lot. Each and every time, these proposals failed because 210 Howard was and remains a very dangerous property to develop for the potential residents of the condominiums, and to the neighborhood residents, especially the neighborhood parents and the kids walking to Beach School. Past Piedmont Planning Commissions and City Council have deemed 210 Howard an unsafe property and have denied projects on the 210 Howard flag lot. But with the invent of SB 9 and Division 17.54, now after almost 25 years of seeing no applications or proposed projects, a developer is back trying to build 4 condominium units, a 4 car garage, 2 30’+/- structures, on a property that a fire truck can’t access. Is there any wonder as to why this application just popped up now? This project may be just the start of an onslaught of SB9/Division 17.54 projects. A Building Permit Review is the place where a project gets looked at for health and safety impacts. Under SB 9/Division 17.54, a project is reviewed for a Building Permit in the 2nd part of a project’s process. But to get to this 2nd part health and safety review, the project must first get approved for a Lot Split and a 2 Two Unit Development. It’s also important to understand that once a project gets this 1st part approval, it’s all downhill for a neighborhood because the developer can go to the County and file for a tentative parcel map. So, where there was once only one parcel, there are now two and a Building Permit is just around the corner. SB 9/ Division 17.54 would like people to think a project can be denied for health and safety impacts, but it requires this very review for health and safety to occur after the project gets approved for a lot split and along with the right to build up to 4 residential units. articles.text: Young Wooly is a one-yearold cream-colored husky mix with a playful and engaging personality who loves both human interaction and canine companionship. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting residents to help make a selection of new playground equipment at Linda Beach Tot Lot. A brief online survey is now available. The survey builds on two recent events at the tot lot where staff spoke to playground users about their preferences and priorities for new playground equipment. The survey invites community members to share: • how often they visit Linda Beach Tot Lot • what age children they bring • what they like most about the Tot Lot • which types of equipment are most important to include • whether they prefer matting or playground “turf” for the new playground surface The survey is available at piedmont.ca.gov/BeachTotLotSurvey and will remain open through February 21. In addition to replacing the aging playground equipment, this project will: • create ADA access from Linda Avenue to the playground • resurface the playground with ADA compliant matting or turf • install a new water fountain or bottle filling station Funding for the project was included in the 2024-25 City budget and includes a $100,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. articles.text: On February 11, the College and Career Center hosted the first annual Open House in the Alan Harvey Theater to show parents and students what the office offers students for individual post-high school planning. On February 27 and 28 students will have more opportunities to learn about specific trades at an open house that will have a young professional panel, a guest speaker and a resume writing workshop. Piedmont and Millennium High counselor Stefanie Manalo-LeClair called the Open House an opportunity for families to see the collaboration that takes place with the academic high school counselors. Open House speakers on February 11 included Assistant Principal Joe Marick and counselors Amanda Carlson, Chris Hartford, and Michelle Hoang. “I believe families [came] away having a general understanding of how students are supported by their counselors, where to find the resources available to them, and hopefully feel a better sense of where to start in this process,” said Manalo-LeClair. At the Open House students were asked “what’s your story?” in relation to writing college essays. articles.text: Astronomers of every stripe are looking forward to next month’s total lunar eclipse, which will be visible from the Bay Area if skies are clear. According to Chabot Space & Science Center astronomer Gerald McKeegan, “There will be a total Lunar Eclipse (a.k.a. Blood Moon) late on the night of Thursday, March 13. The visible part of the eclipse will begin at 10:09 p.m. Pacific Daylight Time. The mid-point of the eclipse will be at 11:59 p.m. (one minute before midnight.) The visible part of the eclipse will end at 1:48 a.m. Friday morning, March 14. NASA’s website advises the best way to view the eclipse: “You don’t need any special equipment to observe a lunar eclipse, although binoculars or a telescope will enhance the view. A dark environment away from bright lights makes for the best viewing conditions. “The same phenomenon that makes our sky blue and our sunsets red causes the Moon to turn reddish-orange during a lunar eclipse. Sunlight appears white, but it actually contains a rainbow of components—and different colors of light have different physical properties. Blue light scatters relatively easily as it passes through Earth’s atmosphere. Reddish light, on the other hand, travels more directly through the air. A “Blood Moon” lunar eclipse is coming in March. When the Sun is high on a clear day, we see blue light scattered throughout the sky overhead. At sunrise and sunset, when the Sun is near the horizon, incoming sunlight travels a longer, low-angle path through Earth’s atmosphere to observers on the ground. The bluer part of the sunlight scatters away in the distance (where it’s still daytime), and only the yellow-to-red part of the spectrum reaches our eyes. During a lunar eclipse, the Moon appears red or orange because any sunlight that’s not blocked by our planet is filtered through a thick slice of Earth’s atmosphere on its way to the lunar surface. It’s as if all the world’s sunrises and sunsets are projected onto the Moon. Chabot Space & Science Center will host a public lunar eclipse viewing event from 9 pm Thursday, March 13, through 1 am Friday, March 14 on its observation deck and telescopes with astronomer presentations, activities for all ages and hot cocoa. For more information and tickets. See http://www.chabotspace.org.

articles.text: Nearly a dozen Girl Scouts from Troop #33521 celebrated their recently completed Silver Awards at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last Wednesday. The 11 Scouts are 9th graders who spent the past three years working towards their Silver Award. The highest honor a Girl Scout Cadette can receive, the Silver Award encourages them to take action and make an impact on their community. To complete their project, each group found a problem they wanted to solve, met with an advisor, and worked towards a solution. The Scouts spent more than 50 hours on their chosen projects, ranging from food insecurity to resources for refugees. Their topics reflect the changes they want to see in the community, and what problems they care about in their own lives. Among the 11 girls, there were six projects: • Annalise Gudiksen, Elsa Chun, and Norah Huang led a Domestic Violence Awareness Club. They created club lesson plans and hung posters around Piedmont Middle School to educate students about domestic violence, self-defense, and healthy relationships. • Rose Reining and Olivia Bailey created a website to provide resources to new pet owners, including information on caring for senior animals and animals with disabilities. • • • • Mina Herrgott and Audrey Levin made brochures, flyers, and a website to encourage community members to donate unpicked fresh fruits and vegetables to organizations helping to fight food insecurity and reduce food waste. Gracey Ann Hatchell painted a mural at Piedmont Middle School to spread awareness about seafood sustainability. Ava Casalaina and Mira Sen created a Newcomer Resource Guide, and distributed it to more than 100 middle and high school-aged refugees and asylum seekers in the Bay Area. Josie Schuetz created a stop motion animation to spread awareness about plastic pollution and how we can fight it. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, February 19, 2025 Piedmont Girl Scouts earn Silver Award By Elsa Chun Nearly a dozen Girl Scouts from Troop #33521 celebrated their recently completed Silver Awards at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last Wednesday. The 11 Scouts are 9th graders who spent the past three years working towards their Silver Award. The highest honor a Girl Scout Cadette can receive, the Silver Award encourages them to take action and make an impact on their community. To complete their project, each group found a problem they wanted to solve, met with an advisor, and worked towards a solution. The Scouts spent more than 50 hours on their chosen projects, ranging from food insecurity to resources for refugees. Their topics reflect the changes they want to see in the community, and what problems they care about in their own lives. Among the 11 girls, there were six projects: • Annalise Gudiksen, Elsa Chun, and Norah Huang led a Domestic Violence Awareness Club. They created club lesson plans and hung posters around Piedmont Middle School to educate students about domestic violence, self-defense, and healthy relationships. • Rose Reining and Olivia Bailey created a website to provide resources to new pet owners, including information on caring for senior animals and animals with disabilities. • • • • Mina Herrgott and Audrey Levin made brochures, flyers, and a website to encourage community members to donate unpicked fresh fruits and vegetables to organizations helping to fight food insecurity and reduce food waste. Gracey Ann Hatchell painted a mural at Piedmont Middle School to spread awareness about seafood sustainability. Ava Casalaina and Mira Sen created a Newcomer Resource Guide, and distributed it to more than 100 middle and high school-aged refugees and asylum seekers in the Bay Area. Josie Schuetz created a stop motion animation to spread awareness about plastic pollution and how we can fight it. articles.text: A teenage pedestrian was stuck by a vehicle at the intersection of Grand and Greenbank Avenues on Tuesday, February 11, around 6:00 p.m. The incident turned into a hit-andrun when the driver of a Ford pickup truck fled the scene after striking the girl. According to police and eyewitnesses, the teenager was hit by a white 1998 Ford F-250 truck. She ended up on the ground 15-feet from where she had been on the sidewalk. The truck proceeded to flee the scene, traveling on the wrong lane of traffic without stopping. The girl was brought to a hospital by paramedics and is in stable condition. The suspect vehicle was quickly identified using the Piedmont Police Department’s Public Safety Camera System and Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras, and the driver was later arrested at his home in San Leandro by two Piedmont Police officers. The suspect, Alfredo SotoReyes, was arrested and sent to Santa Rita Jail. Casey Bivens, a resident of the area, was unloading his car nearby when the collision occurred. “I saw her, just a few feet above the ground, land on the ground. It took maybe three seconds to register what actually happened and what I was looking at,” said Bivens. Bivens provided immediate aid and stayed with the teenager until the paramedics arrived. She was treated and later released. Piedmont Police utilized license plate cameras and public safety cameras to locate the suspect. At 6:33 p.m. the police log shows the suspect vehicle, with front end damage, was located on Lark Street in San Leandro. The registered owner of the truck was contacted at 7:23 p.m. and arrested. The suspect is charged with a felony hit-and-run along with reckless driving and was taken to Santa Rita Jail. Piedmont Captain Chris Monahan gave credit to the use of technology in making the arrest. “It’s another example of the value-add that both the license plate cameras and the public safety cameras bring in our ability to apprehend offenders or those committing crimes in our city,” said Monahan. articles.text: Basketball team falls to Alameda, CV to end regular season Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team wrapped up its regular season with a pair of losses against Western Alameda County conference competition, falling by one point, 59-58, to Castro Valley at home on Friday, February 14, and losing 66-57 to league champions Alameda two days earlier. The pair of games closes Piedmont’s regular season with a 12-14 record. PHS benefitted from its difficult schedule and going 4-0 against other Division 4 schools, earning the No. 1 seed in the D4 North Coast Section bracket. The last time PHS received the top seed was when they won the D4 title in 2020, which was coach Ben Spencer’s first year at the helm. Since winning the D4 title, Piedmont has at least reached the semifinals in three straight tournaments. PHS lost to Branson in the 2022 and 2023 D3 semifinals, while they narrowly lost 65-55 in the D3 Finals to University last year. This marks their first time playing in the D4 bracket since winning it all in 2020. Prior to their game against Castro Valley, Piedmont honored its two seniors on the roster in Ravi Silverberg and Emmet Asulin. Piedmont will host No. 16 Ukiah tonight, February 19, for the opening round. With a win, the Highlanders will host the winner of No. 8 Hayward and No. 9 Bethel. Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg, a three-year starter, played his final regular season game for Piedmont High. 59-58 loss to Castro Valley Piedmont trailed 15-14 through the first quarter, but took a 29-28 lead by halftime. Castro Valley got back to the front in the third quarter by scoring 15 points and allowing 13, making it 43-42 for the Trojans. In the final going, both teams scored 16 points. The Highlanders also lost their first game against Castro Valley by just one point, 50-49, on January 29. Despite the loss, it was an important return for the team’s second-leading scorer, Dillon Casey, who suffered an injury against San Leandro on January 31. Final stats: Ravi Silverberg led with 15 points, Casey scored 13 points, Beach Lorin had 11, Emmet Asulin, a two-year varsity member, wrapped up his regular season career at Piedmont. Dillon Casey returned to Piedmont’s lineup in time for the North Coast Section post-season playoffs.

articles.text: Girls’ basketball team gets No.5 seed in NCS Open Division Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team closed out its regular season at Binks Rawlings Gym with a 72-24 win over Castro Valley on Friday, February 14 and a 74-60 victory over Alameda two days earlier. The pair of wins means they will share the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division first-place banner with Bishop O’Dowd. The Highlanders finished its season with seven straight wins to post a record of 21-4 and 7-1 against league competition, proving to be one of the best teams in the North Coast Section. As a result, they received the No. 5 overall ranking in the Open Division. PHS will travel to Santa Rosa tomorrow to face No. 4 Cardinal Newman tomorrow, February 20. Piedmont’s recent win over Alameda came after holding a 37-31 lead at halftime. The Hornets got the No. 10 seed in Division 1, but in the Open Division, Piedmont will face the section’s best of the best. “What we talked about at halftime and after the game is when we play an Open team, if you’re not alert and ready to play, you can go down by 15. They execute at a higher rate, you have to match that intensity and execution,” said PHS coach Bryan Gardere. It’s an impressive achievement for a team with three freshman as starting varsity players – Jenelle Solis, Andrea Martin, and Savannah Dennig. The team also Shakila Zuberii is a four-year varsity player. Staff Photos Briana Webb, a senior, is finishing up her first year on the varsity squad. includes sophomore Taylor White and first-year varsity starter Briana Webb. “We’re going to play better teams in the Open, so we need to prepare ourselves for this competition. We’re just taking things game by game,” Solis said. Piedmont celebrated Webb and four-year varsity player Shakila Zuberi as its two seniors on the roster prior to their game against Castro Valley,. “It marks the end of my journey, but it’s more of a celebration. Now that its so close, I want to delay it and want more games at home,” Zuberi said. “It means a lot to me. It’s sentimental, but it’s been a hard journey and there’s been a lot of happy moments,” Webb mentioned, who came to Piedmont from Moreau in Hayward.

articles.text: Highlanders earn No. 1 seed in Div. 4 NCS playoffs Photos by Scott Stratman Piedmont honored its 10 seniors on the roster for Senior Night. Pictured are Gianluca Bini (left, #34), Enzo Bernales (front), Bosco Lorin (#50), Harper Man (#35), Logan Faucher (#42), Niko Markopoulos (#22), Jacques Saldanha (#10), Lucas Malecki (goal keeper), Jacob Rodriguez (#9), and Max Goldfarb (#36). The Highlanders’ boys’ soccer team finished up its regular season with a pair of ties against Western Alameda County Conference competition. They tied Castro Valley 2-2 at the Trojans’ home stadium on Thursday, February 13 and drew 0-0 with Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, February 11 at Witter Field. The pair of results brings PHS’ record to 7-4-8 (W-T-L) to end its season. Piedmont benefitted from its difficult schedule, earning the No. 1 seed in the Division 4 North Coast Section bracket and set to host No. 16 Justin-Siena tonight, February 19. Of their games, PHS faced D1 bracket qualifiers Campolindo, Berkeley, and Alameda, along with Tennyson, O’Dowd, Granada, and Mt. Eden of the D2 bracket. The last time PHS received the top seed in the D4 postseason, they won the entire tournament, culminating in a 1-0 win over No. 2 University. It gives Piedmont to win the Division 4 first-place banner for the third time in the last four years after winning the title in 2023 as the No. 8 seed in another 1-nil win over University. Last year, Piedmont bumped up to D3 as the No. 2 seed, but lost in the quarterfinals to Archie Williams. Prior to Tuesday’s tie against Bishop O’Dowd, PHS honored its 10 seniors on the roster for Senior Night, including Lucas Malecki, Jacob Rodriguez, Jacques Saldanha, Niko Markopoulos, Gianluca Bini, Harper Mand, Max Goldfarb, Logan Faucher, Enzo Bernales, and Bosco Lorin. Providing a big boost to the lineup is the return of Bernales for his first game after electing to focus on his MLS Next club team. He was our 2023 Sophomore of the Year. 2-2 tie with Castro Valley Castro Valley opened the game with two early goals within a few minutes of each other in the 12th Logan Faucher scored a goal against Castro Valley.

Overcoming the weather, it defeated the visiting Encinal Jets,3-0, The Highlanders head into the North Coast Section postseason with a 6-2-9 (W-TL) record and attained the No. 1 seed in the Division 4 bracket despite walking in with a losing record. Piedmont hosts No. 16 College Prep tonight, February 19 in its opening game of the playoffs. PHS benefitted from a difficult schedule, where they had narrow 2-1 losses to Campolindo and defending D1 State champions Archbishop Mitty. Campo is the No. 6 seed in the D2 bracket. They also lost to D1 top seed Carondelet and tied 1-1 with D1 No. 8 seed Las Lomas. Earning the top seed is a refreshing benchmark for the squad after having enduring a season ravaged with injuries. Senior captain Louisa Symkowick returned to the lineup against Encinal after missing extended time. Starting center back Eliza Hammond and striker Hannah Sullivan scored against the Jets after also missing games earlier in the season Leading scorer Elsa Wallway suffered a season-ending injury against Berkeley on January 31, while starting center back Darcy McKee went down with a season-ending injury in Piedmont’s very first game. “We scrape into playoffs with our D4 win against Cardinal Newman. It’s been a tough season; injuries have been brutal. Concussions, thigh, quads, ankles, illness. It’s been rough, but tonight was fun. articles.text: Upper Falls is about 15 feet tall; it is situated closely to Basin Falls. [Reprinted from February 2021] Morgan Hill is home to a 1,147 acre park known for its collection of easily accessible waterfalls. On the eastern side of the Santa Cruz Mountains is Uvas Canyon County Park, found at the very end of the private Sveadal community on Croy Road. Hikers will be greeted to the sound of bubbling brooks immediately when entering the park on the Waterfall Loop trail along Swanson Creek. The first and smallest cascade, Granuja Falls, provides a fitting welcome to visitors after the first bridge. After another half mile, hikers will find the base of the Black Rock Falls on the right. Follow the water up the narrow path to find the roughly 20-foot tall waterfall that passes over a black rock face barring its name. Returning back to the Waterfall Loop Trail for just 0.2 of a mile brings walkers to an intersection with the base of Upper Falls on the left, and a walkway to Basin Falls—which seemed to be the most thriving of the park after the rain. Basin Falls stands around 15 feet, flowing down stones as it feeds into Swanson Creek. A fallen tree sits in its center to provide a clear perspective of its size. Returning to the Waterfall loop reunites you with Upper Falls, a two tiered cascade that is also around 15 feet tall. Passing the falls means you are nearing halfway through your day as you venture onto the Contour Trail. The Contour Trail goes for about 1.1 miles and provides some uphill climb to your day, meaning it’s not just a scenic nature hike, but a fitting lower body workout. The trail also surrounds you with the aroma of California Bays, the sprawling red bark of Manzanita, and a towering second-growth redwood here and there. Intersecting with the Alec Canyon Trail, turn right to head just slightly less than a mile to Triple Falls. It’s the final landmark of the day and the tallest of the waterfalls at around 50 feet, but a small trickle compared to the other four. A sixth waterfall is on the right during the main trek in on the Waterfall loop, but it isn’t all the noteworthy given it is a similar small stream and farther away from hikers. Our Uvas Canyon loop to hit every waterfall is approximately 5.2 miles and topped out at 1,273 feet in elevation gain. The Post passed 44 hikers on the day, but over 36 of which came on the initial walk on the Waterfall Loop given its popularity. It is also one of the few dogfriendly parks in the Santa Cruz Mountains, so it is safe to bring your pooch. The park requires 24-hour advance reservations for parking, otherwise you’ll be parking on the road leading in. For parking information, visit https:// parks.sccgov.org/santa-claracounty-parks/uvas-canyon-county-park or search “Uvas Canyon County Park” in your device – it will be the first option in search engines. Punch in “Uvas Canyon County Park” to your GPS device to access this South Bay park. A view of Swanson Creek. You’ll walk over the creek to continue on the Contour Trail.

articles.text: The Batsheva Dance Company will take the stage at Zellerbach Hall with the Bay Area premiere of MOMO this Saturday at 8 p.m. and Sunday at 3 p.m. In the world-renowned company’s own words, this staggering new work by its choreographer Ohad Naharin “has two souls. One sends long roots to the depths of the earth — a soul that embodies archetypes and myths of hardened, raw masculinity, and the other is in a constant search for an individual and distinct DNA. One moves within its own autonomous and independent force field and the other is a constellation of elements that spin around the same nucleus — alternately drifting away and towards it, making room for necessary tenderness and catharsis.” The performance includes recordings of Laurie Anderson and Kronos Quartet’s Landfall, Philip Glass’ Metamorphosis and a song-prayer by the Venezuelan musician Arca, with additional music provided by Naharin himself under the name Maxim Waratt. Of the work, the French newspaper Le Figaro write, “Ohad Naharin’s latest piece is unlike any of his other works … Mesmerizing. And as always, captivating.” The Batsheva Dance Company was founded in 1964 by Baroness Batsheva de Rothschild. Notably, the company was the first outside of American dance maverick Martha Graham’s own troupe to perform her choreography. In its first decades, the company was led by various artistic directors from Israel and abroad. The company has long nurtured a space for creative process and artistic interpretations. Many of its dancers have emerged as creators and choreographers including Bobbi Jene Smith and Or Schraiber, who performed in Olivier Messiaen’s Harawi at Zellerbach Hall earlier this season. Over the course of his years with Batsheva, Naharin has won many awards and honors, among them Chevalier de l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres from the French government, the Samuel H. Scripps American Dance Festival Award for Lifetime Achievement, a Doctor of Philosophy honoris causa by the Hebrew University, and an honorary Doctor of Fine Arts degree from the Juilliard School in New York. In 1990 Ohad Naharin was named artistic director and led the company into a new era. Thanks to his bold choreography, Batsheva Dance Company has been critically acclaimed as one of the foremost contemporary dance companies in the world. The company’s awards and accolades include receipt of the New York Dance and Performance Bessie award, and the Yair Shapira Prize for their contributions to the world of dance. articles.text: The madcap musical comedy Nobody Loves You opens at the American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco on February 28 for a one-month run. The game of love is on: This play features a wildly popular reality dating show by the same name, in which eager contestants compete for love and social media stardom, while audiences are taken on a behind-the-scenes ride through reality television and into real life. When Jeff (A. J. Holmes), a philosophy grad student, snags a spot on the show to win back his ex-girlfriend, he breaks all the rules and tries to blow the game wide open; that is, until he falls for Jenny (Kuhoo Verma), an enticingly prickly producer of the show who yearns to leave the drama to make serious films. In a world where every kiss comes at the end of a selfie stick, can two people really connect? Bay Area hometown heroes Itamar Moses (Tony Award winner for The Band’s Visit, Drama Desk winner for Dead Outlaw) and Gaby Alter provide uproarious screenwriting, witty lyrics, and a winsome pop score in this madcap musical comedy helmed Catch the madcap musical comedy Nobody Loves You at the American Conservatory Theater in San Francisco from February 28 through March 30. by Tony Award winner and A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon. “Nobody Loves You is a hilarious and heartfelt musical quest for authenticity through the ridiculously inauthentic world of a reality dating show,” said MacKinnon. “You will root for your favorites, cringe at their foibles and, by the end of the show, feel that you too should step into the world as yourself and take your chance at love. “Seldom do I laugh as hard as when I get to direct a world created by Itamar Moses,” she added. “I can’t wait to share Nobody Loves You with the Bay Area.” Showtime information and tickets ($25–$130) for the performances at ACT’s Toni Rembe Theatre (415 Geary St., San Francisco) are available at the ACT Box Office at 415-749-2228 or online at act-sf.org/NLY.

articles.text: There’s a lot more to mice than you might think. My predecessors have made exhaustive studies on them. Don’t worry… this story is easy to read even though it delves into philosophy, biography/autobiography, music, and violin making – among many things. Let’s begin by mentioning an important author named Leonard Wibberley. I’ll bet you don’t recognize the name. He was a very interesting character and a brilliant writer to boot. He wrote the book The Mouse that Roared which became a very successful movie and begat many other mouse tales. Wibberley is the subject of this column simply because he was a very interesting character and because I knew him. He was a truly quixotic genius. Being an Irishman, he had many of the characteristics of a leprechaun. As for his gift of words, he was brilliant. Think of Mark Twain in the costume of a leprechaun and you get an inkling. It didn’t matter what the subject was – the result was compelling. Political satire made a lot of money for him. In addition, there were biographies, autobiographies, and many aspects of music. He always wanted to be a violinist, but he was more of a failure than a success. That didn’t seem to matter to him. I used to see him on Saturday mornings in the violin shop of Mario Frosali where he was an apprentice. Most people enjoy being complimented, but not Wibberley. When I told him that I was acquainted with his work and enjoyed it very much you’d think he would be happy. His demeanor changed as if I had insulted him. articles.text: Thursday, Feb. 20 Lage will begin his four-day residency with a 7:30 p.m. solo recital, showcasing the breadth of his guitar mastery in the most revealing setting — one in which his peerless musicianship is presented without restrictions, undiluted and unadorned. The evening will harken back to Lage’s landmark 2015 release World’s Fair, a solo guitar session of original compositions focused on the exploration of the song styles that shaped his own aesthetic, inspired by the work of a formative influence, classical guitar genius Andrés Segovia. Friday, Feb, 21 Night two brings a concert of duets with Jorge Roeder, a longtime collaborator with Lage and among the most acclaimed bassists in modern music. Hailing from Lima, Peru, Roeder began classical cello and bass studies at age 14 and was the assistant principal bassist for the Lima Symphony by 21. Among the first musicians he met when arriving in New York in 2007 were Julian Lage and virtuoso pianist Shai Maestro, who have been long-term musical partners ever since. Saturday, Feb. 22, 7:30 p.m. Lage will bring a program of music including material from his new album Speak To Me with his current working trio including longtime bassist Jorge Roeder and drummer Kenny Wollesen. For this special night, the band is joined by keyboard master John Medeski, best known as one-third of the jazz-funk trio Medeski Martin & Wood and for his work with John Scofield, John Zorn, Robert Randolph, and the Dirty Dozen Brass Band. Speak To Me is Lage’s fourth album for the Blue Note label, produced by the acclaimed singer-songwriter and guitarist Joe Henry and featuring an expansive new set of original songs with guest appearances from saxophonist Levon Henry and keyboard wizard Patrick Warren. Sunday, Feb. 23 Lage’s final night pairs him with the iconoclastic guitarist Marc Ribot. A singular instrumentalist, Ribot follows his muse wherever it leads, resulting in a career that has ranged across free jazz, no-wave, rock, film music and Cuban rumba. Beyond his wildly eclectic output as a leader — which has veered from the rollicking Los Cubanos Postizos to avant-rock to a solo guitar score to accompaniments for Charlie Chaplin’s silent classic The Kid — Ribot is best known as a key collaborator with Tom Waits, Elvis Costello, John Zorn, the Lounge Lizards, Diana Krall, Robert Plant and Alison Krauss.

articles.text: Ralph Fiennes in Conclave Conclave, the recipient of eight 2025 Oscar nominations, to include Best Picture, achieves what film does best: it takes the audience inside one of the world’s most secretive and centuries-old traditions. The church’s Cardinals, dressed in black and scarlet vestments, each with a large Pontifical cross, have been called to the Vatican from around the world. There they will gather behind locked doors in a cloistered conclave, tasked with the responsibility of selecting a new pope. Chosen to manage this densely ritualistic process is Cardinal Lawrence (Ralph Fiennes); his responsibility, we soon realize, is no small endeavor. The position of Pope is not only one of shepherding the millions of Catholics word wide, but one of power. Which Cardinal will be chosen, using paper ballots, while solemn is, as the narrative reveals, also Machiavellian, even touched by scandal and deception. With quiet sidebars, it can seem closely similar to a political gathering of sorts, these small huddles taking place behind closed doors or small huddles. These men of insistent faith are also just men who deal in the currency of secrets, touched by temptation, often conflicted when tested. Conclave is, ultimately, a captivating character study of Cardinal Lawrence who must reach beyond the conclave as he urgently attempts to discover the truth behind two whispered mysteries. This takes place while ballots are filled out and counted as the conclave waits to reach that necessary majority, and a plume of white smoke can be released from the much-watched chimney, signaling that a new pope has finally been elected. Conclave . Directed by Edward Berger. Starring Ralph Fiennes, John Lithgow, Stanly Tucci. 2 hrs. Rated PG. Released in 2024. Streaming on Netflix/ Prime/Fandango/apple tv.

articles.text: Kevin Costner in For Love of the Game For Love of the Game is, indeed, about baseball. But, like so many sports films, the field of play is also a perfect crucible in which the character of those who play are tested. The opening scenes find Billy Chapel (Kevin Costner), veteran Detroit Tigers’ pitcher, waiting in his NYC hotel suite for Jane Aubrey (Kelly Preston). They have agreed to have dinner and (it’s implied) perhaps reconnect after what has been a tumultuous five-year relationship. Jane fails to show up, which is only obliquely explained the next morning. She tearfully tells Billy that she is leaving, having taken a job in London. And it’s at this point that the structure of the film is revealed, one that is ideal for storytelling. Billy is slated to pitch against the Yankees that evening and it’s when he takes the mound to begin what might be the conclusion to an extraordinary career that the writers, using a seamless story-telling device, the flashbacks, which consist of vignettes, beginning with how Jane and Billy meet-cute. This is, after all, far more than a baseball story. And so the actual game begins to take form, inning after inning, the momentum broken only by Billy’s almost meditative reflections on the past. All of this is framed by the inevitable decision facing Chapel regarding his career. He loves the game, deeply, a game he has played almost all of his life, to include 19 years in the big show with the Tigers. To go beyond what I’ve written above would deprive you, the audience, of the enjoyment of watching what I judge to be such a remarkable story, one that transcends the field of play. At the same time, know that the game unfolding, with Billy on the mound throwing hard to his long-time friend and catcher, Gus Simski (John C. Reilly), is standalone riveting. For Love of the Game. articles.text: Life’s work of famous Iranian-American artists on view Through this Sunday, February 23, see two solo exhibitions at San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Center for the Arts that offer investigative portraits of artists whose lives and creative outlets become inextricably linked to political revolution. In the presentation of distinct bodies of work through Nicky Nodjoumi: The Personal is Political and Nahid Hagigat: Etched in Time, visitors will explore the practices of two of the most influential Iranian-American artists today, ranging from Nodjoumi’s surreal and kaleidoscopic paintings exploring manifestations of political power, to Hagigat’s evocative and intimate etchings about women and their ongoing struggle for freedom in Iran. Both exhibitions will be framed by an introductory gallery featuring family photos and archival material shedding light on the personal and shared struggles that shaped these artists’ lives. Nicky Nodjoumi presents a series of paintings created over the past 15 years. In these works, Nodjoumi presents layered narratives that reiterate his staunch commitment to democracy. Exploring the dynamics of power, often through satire, Nodjoumi transforms his lived experiences in Iran and the U.S. into scenes that resonate beyond specific geographical boundaries. His works are like theatrical stages where compositions of figures, both serious and ridiculous, are brought together into stories that illuminate both Nodjoumi’s personal history, and historical experiences of political struggle. Nahid Hagigat offers an evocative selection of paintings, prints and etchings that span six decades. Hagigat explores the constraints of politics and ideologies on women, through works that portray female Iranian figures through a feminist lens. Among these works is a series from the 1970s inspired by photographs sent to Hagigat in New York by her sister in Tehran. Drawing on these images, Hagigat creates scenes of women, children and everyday life, synthesizing history with her personal experience in Iran and New York, moving seamlessly between the personal and the global using images of pain, uncertainty, light, and clarity as a way of moving between the past, present and future. The dual exhibitions are inspired by the film A Revolution on Canvas, an HBO documentary produced by Nodjoumi and Hagigat’s daughter Sara Nodjoumi and her partner Till Schauder. The film begins by investigating the disappearance of 120 of Nodjoumi’s artworks in Tehran after his 1980 exhibition, which led to his family’s exile from their native country. Through an attempt to find the missing paintings, Sara Nodjoumi and Schauder present a layered exploration of her family’s history, her parents’ individual work as artists and the indelible impact of politics on their lives. “These two exhibitions invite us to reflect on the role of artists and the power of creative expression, especially during times of political upheaval,” said YBCA curator Amy Kisch. “How do their voices ground us in our shared humanity? articles.text: A look back at The Maze, now Witter Field English gardens designed as mazes were highly popular in the early 20th Century. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on June 10, 2020. The ninth and final marker in Piedmont Park’s history trail may be the most exotic of them all, The Hedge Maze. The Maze perplexed its visitors in the location now occupied by Piedmont High School’s Witter Field. Marker 9: The Maze The marker is located near Wildwood Ave. overlooking Witter Field. As Frank C. Havens began to expand Piedmont Springs Park, he added The Maze, a playful feature on a grand scale in 1904. The living hedge maze was modeled on the maze at England’s Hampton Court, the home of Henry VIII. Gardeners planted hedges and let time grow them tall to make the maze even more mysterious. Havens developed a lower entrance pathway to Piedmont Park shrouded by palm trees from Grand Avenue, what is now Palm Drive. The prime feature from the lower entrance was The Maze, situated in the natural bowl shaped ravine. A field of roses stood next to The Maze, making this area of Piedmont Park ideal for strolling visitors. The finish line of The Maze was its center, occupied by a red-roofed pagoda. Ladders were placed throughout The Maze to give direction to those who had become lost. Getting to the center was only half the challenge; making it back out could take just as long. A 1914 article in the Oakland Herald noted, “At the western end of the park on the low grounds is situated the “Maze” where the visitor can find much enjoyment trying to find his or her way out to the open path. Here are circles, semicircles and long straight rows of ornamental shrubbery, palms, flowers and deciduous trees. Through this charming spot wind roads of red stone, over which an occasional automobile goes whirling, leaving the trail of gasoline smell to drive away for a moment the delicious odor of pine and redwood.” In 1916 Havens ran into financial trouble so he attempted to sell his ownership of the park to pay his debts. The Oakland Tribune reported that with $90,000 in lawsuit settlements, Havens began to default on the $172,000 mortgage of the park. The school board of Piedmont eventually bought half of the land in 1921, and Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander purchased the other half. The school board used its 13 acres of the park for a new school and a sports field. Alexander was later reimbursed by the city for the other 14 acres, which remained park land. The Maze was demolished in 1920, after entertaining guests for 16 years. Howard Gilkey, a landscape architect, designed the new sports field for the high school. At the time it consisted of a football field with a quarter-mile oval track and a baseball field. In 1948, the high school athletic field received the name Witter Field, in honor of Jean C. Witter, a former captain of the football team who was killed on a destroyer in the U.S. Navy in World War II. After the naming ceremony the first night football game in the East Bay was played with the installation of stadium lights. The Maze represented the archetypical leisurely structure of Piedmont in the days when Piedmont Park was the defining feature of a young city trying to lure tourists’ eyes. Information provided by Gail Lombardi and The Piedmont Historical Society. For more information, see: piedmonthistorical. org. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, February 19, 2025 Following the History Markers in Piedmont Park A look back at The Maze, now Witter Field English gardens designed as mazes were highly popular in the early 20th Century. By Jay Russell Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on June 10, 2020. The ninth and final marker in Piedmont Park’s history trail may be the most exotic of them all, The Hedge Maze. The Maze perplexed its visitors in the location now occupied by Piedmont High School’s Witter Field. Marker 9: The Maze The marker is located near Wildwood Ave. overlooking Witter Field. As Frank C. Havens began to expand Piedmont Springs Park, he added The Maze, a playful feature on a grand scale in 1904. The living hedge maze was modeled on the maze at England’s Hampton Court, the home of Henry VIII. Gardeners planted hedges and let time grow them tall to make the maze even more mysterious. Havens developed a lower entrance pathway to Piedmont Park shrouded by palm trees from Grand Avenue, what is now Palm Drive. The prime feature from the lower entrance was The Maze, situated in the natural bowl shaped ravine. A field of roses stood next to The Maze, making this area of Piedmont Park ideal for strolling visitors. The finish line of The Maze was its center, occupied by a red-roofed pagoda. Ladders were placed throughout The Maze to give direction to those who had become lost. Getting to the center was only half the challenge; making it back out could take just as long. A 1914 article in the Oakland Herald noted, “At the western end of the park on the low grounds is situated the “Maze” where the visitor can find much enjoyment trying to find his or her way out to the open path. Here are circles, semicircles and long straight rows of ornamental shrubbery, palms, flowers and deciduous trees. Through this charming spot wind roads of red stone, over which an occasional automobile goes whirling, leaving the trail of gasoline smell to drive away for a moment the delicious odor of pine and redwood.” In 1916 Havens ran into financial trouble so he attempted to sell his ownership of the park to pay his debts. The Oakland Tribune reported that with $90,000 in lawsuit settlements, Havens began to default on the $172,000 mortgage of the park. The school board of Piedmont eventually bought half of the land in 1921, and Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander purchased the other half. The school board used its 13 acres of the park for a new school and a sports field. Alexander was later reimbursed by the city for the other 14 acres, which remained park land. The Maze was demolished in 1920, after entertaining guests for 16 years. Howard Gilkey, a landscape architect, designed the new sports field for the high school. At the time it consisted of a football field with a quarter-mile oval track and a baseball field. In 1948, the high school athletic field received the name Witter Field, in honor of Jean C. Witter, a former captain of the football team who was killed on a destroyer in the U.S. Navy in World War II. After the naming ceremony the first night football game in the East Bay was played with the installation of stadium lights. The Maze represented the archetypical leisurely structure of Piedmont in the days when Piedmont Park was the defining feature of a young city trying to lure tourists’ eyes. articles.text: Italian Sausage and Garbanzo Bean Soup Photo by Deborah Quok • It’s still soup season, although it’s fair to say soup is welcomed pretty much year-round here in the Bay Area. With those record cold days lately, we’ve been enjoying this simple and satisfying soup, especially at lunchtime. We enjoy it for lunch since it comes together with just a few ingredients you may already have on hand. It’s ready in about 30 minutes, or less, from chopping to serving. My pantry always has low-sodium chicken stock or broth and canned beans on the shelves. Similarly, I always keep a few varieties of fully cooked sausage on hand. The ones I buy are vacuum packed so they store well in the refrigerator, and an even longer life in the freezer. Having these on hand mean I have myriad options for pulling together a tasty meal in short order. Don’t be shy about “doctoring” a store-bought broth. Adding aromatics (onion, garlic, leeks, ginger), fresh or dried herbs, and spices is pretty much mandatory for a soup of any cuisine. For this soup, a bay leaf, oregano and thyme would be delicious additions. Using different sausages, beans, and greens is highly encouraged. Adding cubes of butternut squash would be right in line, too. I highly recommend adding a crunch-factor in the form of croutons (see photo) to bring a tasty, textual component. Making your own is easy; fair warning: you may never go back to store-bought once you’ve made your own. • • • • • • • • 1 can garbanzo beans, rinsed and drained 2 cups lacinato kale, sliced in 1/2-inch strips 1 white onion, small, diced; about 3/4 cup 3/4 cup fresh tomato, diced (Substituting canned diced tomatoes is fine.) 1 clove garlic, minced 1 quart chicken broth, preferably homemade, but low-sodium if store-bought 1 tablespoon olive oil Red chile flakes, to taste Salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste. INSTRUCTIONS Italian Sausage and Garbanzo Bean Soup Makes about 2 quarts INGREDIENTS • 2 links Italian sausage, fully cooked, sliced Heat the olive oil over medium heat in a 3-quart saucepan for about one minute, add the sliced Italian sausage and spread into a single layer. Let brown slightly, then turn to brown the second side, about 3–4 minutes. Add the diced onion and minced garlic and stir to combine. Continue cooking over medium heat until the onion turns translucent. Do not over-brown and be especially watchful of the garlic. Add the diced tomatoes, garbanzo beans and chicken broth. Bring to a gentle boil for at least five minutes to cook the tomatoes. Add the kale and cook until just wilted. Taste and season to taste. Easy Croutons This soup is rustic and begs for big, crunchy croutons atop to provide a textural contrast. For one cup of rustic croutons, simply hand pull 1/2 – 1-inch chunks of bread from your favorite loaf and toss in about 1–2 tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.

articles.text: It was a cool and overcast afternoon on February 3rd when the First Mondays Reading Group met for their monthly discussion at the Community Hall. There was a good turnout of 21 readers on hand for the meeting. The readers tried something new at this meeting. The group has grown significantly since it started in January 2019. Currently, 68 people are registered with the Recreation Department for the activity. There have been as many as 25 participants in individual discussions, and some readers had a desire for a smaller group. As an experiment, chairs were set up in the Community Hall alcove for a smaller conversation. Six readers went off to the smaller session, and the rest of the group stayed in the hall’s main room. Lois Price led the smaller discussion, while Priscilla Wanerus continued to lead the bigger group. The English cookies that Carol Long brought were enjoyed by both groups. The readers were there to talk about their February book, Endurance: Shackleton’s Incredible Voyage by Alfred Lansing. It was written in 1959 and is the story of the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, led by Sir Ernest Shackleton, and its failed attempt to cross the Antarctic continent in 1914. Lansing tells the story of an almost two-year struggle for survival endured by the Endurance’s twenty-eight man crew. This exploration ship became stuck in and eventually crushed by Antarctic ice, leaving the men stranded on the pack ice. The crew drifted on ice floes for over a year in desperately cold conditions. They lived off the ship’s dwindling provisions and the seals and other animals they killed. Finally, Shackleton and a few of his crew barely reached South Georgia Island 650 nautical miles away. Shackleton then led two of them on the first successful overland crossing of South Georgia. Three months later, he was able to rescue the remaining crew members. Almost every diary from the expedition was made available to Lansing, and almost all the surviving crew members provided lengthy interviews. Lansing drew on these resources to make the book’s characters very personal and his account very real. This is a survival story. Almost all the book deals with the hardships the Endurance’s crew experienced. Their constant suffering can be hard for the reader, but the book was well received by the group. For some it was a surprise. They wouldn’t have picked the book, but once they started it, they couldn’t put this adventure story down. Some felt the book might not be great literature, but it is well-written, absorbing, and a little gruesome. The frigid cold and hardships that Shakleton and his crew experienced were an endless procession of misery. The Endurance’s crew were seamen. They knew they were signing up for a long and dangerous expedition, and they were well prepared, but this voyage was more than anyone expected. The readers admired and were amazed by the ability of all these men to survive their ordeal. How did they stay sane? How did they avoid hypothermia? How did they stay focused and together? Shakleton’s leadership was a major part of their survival. The readers were impressed by him and his determination to save his crew. Endurance is a good study of leadership. The readers were asked, “Could a crew today do Alfred Lansing’s Endurance tells the story of an almost two-year struggle for survival endured by the Endurance’s twenty-eight man crew. what these early 20th Century men did?” Yes, they thought, if they were the right crew and had the right leadership. After separate discussions the two groups rejoin for the remainder of the meeting for a recap and the selection of their next book. The participants in the smaller group discussion felt it was a success. It was flexible, conversational, and the acoustics were better. So, the intent is that a smaller, separate group will be part of future meetings. The group had previously selected James by Percival Everett for March, and Nasty, Brutish, and Short: Adventures in Philosophy with My Kids by Scott Hershovitz for their April book. After Laura Goldman’s presentation of three fiction candidates for their May book, the readers selected Cloudstreet by Tim Winton. articles.text: A strong turnout of 48 walkers and three K-9 best friends were on hand at the Exedra to get their steps before the rain. Pala, Mesa, and Monte Avenues, just above Highland Avenue, were nearby streets the group could walk, and they could then climb the steps between Pala and Scenic Avenue to see views of the Bay and the looming clouds. The walkers went up Highland Avenue, turned up Oakland Avenue, and stopped in front of the house on the corner. This Victorian was built by John Rackliffe and his wife Ellen in 1899. Rackliffe was 73 years at the time but needed a large house for his family that included his two adult children and a grandson. The Rackliffes were one of the few families listed in the 1900 Piedmont Census. The house’s cross gabled roof and octagonal corner turret with gables of different sizes and a witch cap roof are typical of Queen Anne designs of the period. Jim Kellogg pointed out the seamless addition that architect Grier Graff later designed for the home. The area above Oakland and Highland Avenues was a bit of a bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters, including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there and before them land developer Frank C. Havens also resided in this area. Many of the homes in this neighborhood were built soon after the San Francisco Earthquake. After Piedmont became an incorporated city in 1907, home construction boomed. The homes were built above an early pathway that went from Moraga Avenue to the one-room cabin of Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area. Blair named the path “Vernal” because of the abundant ferns and shrubs that grew around a nearby spring. That roadway was renamed “Highland Avenue” in 1911. The homes built above the street were part of the Alta Piedmont Track and Alta Heights development of Wick ham Havens, Frank C.’s son. The walkers wondered if Wickham’s “Alta Piedmont” resulted in later references to “Baja Piedmont” for the streets below Highland. The group went up Oakland Avenue, turned left on the oneblock Hardwick Avenue, and walked to Blair Avenue. They went up Pala, turned on Mesa and enjoyed the attractive homes built in Bungalow, American Foursquare, Colonial Revival, and Craftsman styles. Seven homes on Mesa’s were built in 1907, The walkers took special notice of the home at 17 Mesa. Its exterior ornamentation is unique with lovely, miniature columns supporting large, curved brackets on the porch. The group went up Moraga Avenue to Monte and back to Pala. The homes along Monte were built between 1906 and 1960. The walkers stopped to appreciate another beautiful home, this one at 110 Monte. Its design is interesting and complex with a hipped roof, twin towers, stained glass windows, and a red tiled roof in an unusual L-shaped design with varied roof heights. The walkers went up Pala to the Scenic-Pala Steps, 161 feet to the top. On Scenic they enjoyed an expansive, cloudy view of the Bay. They continued up the street and marveled at homes built on Scenic’s steep ridge above Blair Park and Moraga Avenue below. Even more surprising were story poles on a vacant lot indicating a new home is planned for the steep slope. Further up Scenic the group passed the longest path in Piedmont, the 281-foot steps down to Blair. The group’s return to the Exedra was via Alta Avenue, Blair, Pacific, Mountain, and Highland Avenues with more beautiful, cloudy views along the way. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Jorge Alberto Eduardo Suarez Rivas, Jr., age 54, passed away at home in Fairfield, California on February 3, 2025 of natural causes. A native of Piedmont, Jorge was born on February 20, 1970, in San Francisco, California, to Linda Fraizer Suarez Rivas and Jorge Alberto Eduardo Suarez Rivas, Sr. He was a graduate of Piedmont High School and received his Bachelor of Arts degree in History from Saint Mary’s College in Moraga. A dedicated employee of Southern Wine & Spirits for nearly 20 years, he was the East Bay District Manager at the time of his passing. In his youth, Jorge worked as a bartender in the Bay Area and Pasadena, and was well known as a craft cocktail specialist (before anybody knew what that meant), creating many oneof-a-kind drinks, including the classic, “Jorge’s Headbanger.” Jorge was fiercely proud of his Cuban heritage and served as the unofficial family armchair genealogist and collector of stories. He often spoke with great admiration of his father, Jorge, and Uncles Eduardo and Juan, for their participation in the Bay of Pigs Invasion in 1961. All three men were captured and tortured by Castro’s forces and spent nearly two years in Cuban prisoner camps. Jorge was a salesperson extraordinaire. winning countless awards and accolades. He was a loving and fun grandfather, and drenched participants in the notorious El Cerrito Avenue water balloon fights on Memorial Day weekends of long ago. Christmas Day will never be the same without Jorge hosting the annual family dinner at a Chinese restaurant in Walnut Creek. Most importantly, he was a devoted husband, father, grandfather, son, brother, Piedmont native Jorge Suarez Rivas, Jr. died on February 3 at age 54. uncle and friend. Jorge was beloved by family, friends and colleagues, and his sudden passing has been devastating to all who knew him. He is survived by his wife, Diane Suarez Rivas, daughters, Jennifer (Riki) Barulich and Julia (Patrick) Mullaney; son, Daniel Brown; grandchildren, Quinn Barulich, Emilia Barulich, Kiera Mullaney, Jack Mullaney, Rudy Brown, Logan Brown, and Callie Brown; mother, Linda Fraizer Ruby; sister, Tana Suarez Rivas (David Shall); brother, Matthew Ruby (Lisa Billings); nephew, Rocco Ruby; godson, Parker Gneckow; beloved dog, Charlotte, and many aunts, uncles and cousins. He was predeceased by his father, Jorge Alberto Eduardo Suarez Rivas, Sr.; stepfather, Robert L. Ruby; and grandparents, Eduardo Suarez Rivas, Ofelia Munroe, and Margurite and Keith Fraizer. A Celebration of Life will be on Friday, March 14, at 2:00 p.m., at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont.

Beyond is India. How they accomplish this remarkable feat makes for an astonishing tale, not unlike in some strange way the survival tale 127 Hours. Both experiences are testimony to the depth of the very human desire to survive. While 127 Hours is relatively static and claustrophobic, No Way Back is all about movement and space, filling the screen with vistas that are startling in their seemingly benign beauty, though clearly malevolent in their raw harshness and inherent deprivations. The performances by the international ensemble are outstanding, led by Harris as a stoic American engineer who came to a background on land and sea that is lush with a rainbow of colors. Regarding the characters, each is a wonderful creation of movement and expression. But with that said, and filled with anticipation and promise, Moana 2 abruptly shifts and becomes just another movie, much to my disappointment. The slow island story morphs into a series of slapstick scenes, some verging on the manic. Indeed, the crew now includes the familiar presence on board of Maui (Dwayne Johnson), covered in his familiar animated and responsive tattoos. It’s as if the writers decided that in order to hold the attention of the young audience, well, they needed to pump up the volume and increase the pace, beginning with the crew arriving at an island inhabited by a gnarly, angry tribe of half-shelled coconuts called Kakamonas. articles.text: Prior to 1922, a largely neglected park with a rustic Japanese tea house and a bandstand sat on land that had originally been owned by Frank C. Havens. That year, the City of Piedmont acquired the land and engaged architect Albert Farr to design a civic center. His elaborate plan featured a Spanish Colonial design that included the Community Hall, a rose garden, expansive lawns, and the iconic Exedra. Funded by a bond issue, the construction of both the Exedra and the Community Hall began in 1924 and was completed in 1925, marking their 100th anniversary this year. Unfortunately, the Great Depression soon followed, halting the completion of Farr’s grand design. How fortunate for Piedmont to have these two incredible structures. The term “Exedra,” originating from ancient Greek, is defined by Webster as “a room, building or outdoor area with seating, where conversations were held.” Piedmont’s Exedra is that, and much more than just a place to sit and talk. The front of the Exedra has remained unchanged, still featuring its distinctive iron gates and blue vase. The area behind the Exedra, however, has seen significant improvements over the years and much of that is thanks to the dedication of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. ing signs of age. That September, the City accepted a generous gift of over $26,000 from PBF to restore the Exedra “to its original elegance”. PBF also agreed to oversee the project. Under the leadership of PBF President Barbara Magee, a committee was formed with Bob Leefeldt, former Chair of the Park Commission, at the helm. The restoration work was meticulous, including the use of epoxy injections to patch and seal cracks in the walls. It was believed this material would be more flexible and durable than plaster. Research was also undertaken to find a paint that would be resistant to graffiti. The most challenging part of the project was repairing the iron gates, which required an additional $15,000 in fundraising. The project was so delicate that Leefeldt had to present his plans to the City Council for approval. Leefeldt told the Council, “The gates were assembled like a fine Swiss watch.” The gates were removed carefully, treated with brushed steel material, and then reinstalled. Forty-five years later, the restoration has stood the test of time. During this period, PBF has played a significant role enhancing the area behind the Exedra with several important projects. In 2001 the Matthew Lempres Memorial Fund and the Marianne Lempres Memorial Fund provided support for a beautiful fountain and a terrace of tiles, as well as seating areas. These additions have transformed the space into a delightful spot for conversation – true to the Exedra’s ancient Greek meaning. In 2008 the Barbara Magee Overlook was dedicated with steps down to the plateau overlooking Bushy Dell Creek and the canyon. This project honored Magee’s contributions to both the Exedra’s renovation and other initiatives during her presidency of PBF and many years as an advisor. Shortly afterwards, a special moonlighting installation from the Exedra to the Magee Overlook was completed in memory of Frances Bishopric, another longtime PBF advisor. But the most special thing about Piedmont’s Exedra is that it has become much more than a place to sit and have conversations. Today the Exedra is a symbol of the City itself—rivaling the thistle which adorns the City’s white flag. Its location in front of a graceful crescent of Highland Poplar Trees (named as Heritage Trees in 2019) together with the planting circle, often filled with purple and white flowers, stands as a perfect focal point as one walks or drives down Highland Avenue to the center of town. In 2002, under the leadership of then President Betty Shapiro, PBF adopted the Exedra as its logo. Various depictions had appeared on earlier PBF documents, but in 2002 the present version became official. {More recently a brandnew on-line newspaper chose the name “The Exedra.”} In fact, images of the Exedra pop up here and there all over the City.
